steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on speeding up model evaluations in uncertainty propagation on tensor grids using computational graph transformations (AMTC). Introduce forward UQ and the main non-intrusive methods, explain the waste in full-grid evaluations, present our method, and outline the paper.

- Uncertainty propagation (forward UQ) and its applications
- Sources of uncertainty and the problem setting
- Common non-intrusive UQ methods

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Forward UQ
  - numerical models never perfectly match reality; inherent uncertainties
  - uncertainty propagation / forward UQ: how outputs are influenced by input uncertainties
  - supports informed decision-making, risk assessment
  - applications: weather forecast, structural analysis, aircraft design (cite each)
- Uncertainty types and setting
  - aleatoric: irreducible, intrinsic (operational conditions, mission prerequisites, model parameters); probabilistic description
  - epistemic: reducible, knowledge gaps, approximations in models/numerical methods; hard to describe probabilistically
  - focus: probabilistic formalism, continuous random inputs with known densities
  - goal: mean, variance of Quantity of Interest (QoI); risk measures like probability of failure, conditional value at risk
- Non-intrusive methods: method of moments, polynomial chaos, kriging, Monte Carlo
  - moments: Taylor series, evaluations + derivatives at one/few points (cite); first (cite) or second order (cite); efficient for moments, not other risk measures; inaccurate with large input variance
  - Monte Carlo: random sampling; law of large numbers, rate independent of dimension -> high-dim; multi-fidelity (cite), importance sampling (cite); many more evaluations in low dim
  - kriging = Gaussian process regression; surrogate from input-output pairs; reliability analysis (cite), optimization under uncertainty (cite)
  - polynomial chaos: low-dim, smooth -> most efficacious; orthogonal polynomials from input distributions; fast convergence; NIPC (cite), SC (cite)
- Tensor grids
  - NIPC and SC can sample with tensor-product grid; points grow exponentially with number of inputs -> only very low-dim
  - common: sparse grids or random points
  - our finding: keeping tensor structure has advantages; cost can be reduced differently
- Wasteful evaluations
  - model as computational graph of elementary operations
  - each operation evaluated at all tensor-product points
  - outputs only distinct at distinct points of its dependent input space; many operations don't depend on all inputs -> waste
- AMTC
  - Accelerated Model evaluations on Tensor grids using Computational graph transformations
  - modifies graph to remove unnecessary evaluations in integration-based NIPC and SC
  - partition graph into sub-graphs by dependency; evaluate each on distinct quadrature points
  - implemented with Computational System Design Language (CSDL); general, automatic
  - applied to four UQ problems; three show significant acceleration with full-grid NIPC -> most efficient implemented method
  - expected for multi-point, multi-disciplinary, sparse-graph models; NIPC and SC and beyond
  - outline: Section 2 background; Section 3 AMTC and CSDL; Section 4 results on three problems; Section 5 conclusions

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
In practice, numerical models can never match reality perfectly and they always have to deal with inherent uncertainties. To address this, uncertainty propagation, which is also called forward uncertainty quantification (UQ), tries to rigorously examine and analyze how the output of a system is influenced by the uncertainties in its inputs. The uncertainty assessments that come out of this are a valuable basis for informed decision-making and thorough risk assessment. UQ is applied in many scientific and engineering domains, for example weather forecast, structural analysis and aircraft design.

The uncertainties in the inputs can come from different origins, and they are usually classified into two categories, aleatoric and epistemic. Aleatoric uncertainties are known as irreducible uncertainties. They are intrinsic to the system and include things like fluctuations in operational conditions, mission prerequisites and model parameters, and they can often be described in a probabilistic framework. Epistemic uncertainties on the other hand are reducible uncertainties that come from gaps in knowledge. They can be caused by approximations used in computational models or numerical solution methods, and they are often hard to describe in a probabilistic framework. In this paper we focus on UQ problems in a probabilistic formalism, where the uncertain inputs are continuous random variables with known probability density distributions. The goal is to estimate statistical moments like the mean and variance of the Quantity of Interest (QoI), or more complex risk measures like the probability of failure or the conditional value at risk.

For this kind of UQ problem, the most common non-intrusive methods are the method of moments, polynomial chaos, kriging, and Monte Carlo. The method of moments computes the statistical moments of the QoI analytically with a Taylor series approximation. It often only uses function evaluations and derivative information at one input point or a small number of them. The variants used most often use derivatives up to first or second order so that they stay cost-effective. This approach is efficient at estimating statistical moments, but it has difficulties estimating other kinds of risk measures, and it can be inaccurate when the input variance is large. The Monte Carlo approach instead samples the uncertain inputs randomly to compute the risk measures. Because of the law of large numbers, the convergence rate of Monte Carlo does not depend on the number of uncertain inputs, so it is particularly attractive for high-dimensional problems. Recent work to make it more efficient includes multi-fidelity and importance sampling techniques. But for low-dimensional problems, Monte Carlo can need many more model evaluations to get the same accuracy as the other UQ methods. Kriging, which is also known as Gaussian process regression, is a common statistical technique used in many fields. In UQ, kriging builds a surrogate response surface from input-output data pairs. The surrogate model replaces the original expensive function so that a large number of model evaluations can be done for reliability analysis or optimization under uncertainty. For low-dimensional UQ problems, if we assume the objective function is smooth, polynomial chaos-based techniques are often the most efficacious option. Generalized polynomial chaos theory represents the QoI with orthogonal polynomials derived from the distributions of the uncertain inputs. Since the random space is smooth, polynomial chaos-based methods converge fast with sampling or integration techniques. Common polynomial chaos-based methods are non-intrusive polynomial chaos (NIPC) and stochastic collocation (SC).

- Tensor grids
  - NIPC and SC can sample with tensor-product grid; points grow exponentially with number of inputs -> only very low-dim
  - common: sparse grids or random points
  - our finding: keeping tensor structure has advantages; cost can be reduced differently
- Wasteful evaluations
  - model as computational graph of elementary operations
  - each operation evaluated at all tensor-product points
  - outputs only distinct at distinct points of its dependent input space; many operations don't depend on all inputs -> waste
- AMTC
  - Accelerated Model evaluations on Tensor grids using Computational graph transformations
  - modifies graph to remove unnecessary evaluations in integration-based NIPC and SC
  - partition graph into sub-graphs by dependency; evaluate each on distinct quadrature points
  - implemented with Computational System Design Language (CSDL); general, automatic

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
In practice, numerical models can never match reality perfectly and they always have to deal with inherent uncertainties. To address this, uncertainty propagation, which is also called forward uncertainty quantification (UQ), tries to rigorously examine and analyze how the output of a system is influenced by the uncertainties in its inputs. The uncertainty assessments that come out of this are a valuable basis for informed decision-making and thorough risk assessment. UQ is applied in many scientific and engineering domains, for example weather forecast, structural analysis and aircraft design.

The uncertainties in the inputs can come from different origins, and they are usually classified into two categories, aleatoric and epistemic. Aleatoric uncertainties are known as irreducible uncertainties. They are intrinsic to the system and include things like fluctuations in operational conditions, mission prerequisites and model parameters, and they can often be described in a probabilistic framework. Epistemic uncertainties on the other hand are reducible uncertainties that come from gaps in knowledge. They can be caused by approximations used in computational models or numerical solution methods, and they are often hard to describe in a probabilistic framework. In this paper we focus on UQ problems in a probabilistic formalism, where the uncertain inputs are continuous random variables with known probability density distributions. The goal is to estimate statistical moments like the mean and variance of the Quantity of Interest (QoI), or more complex risk measures like the probability of failure or the conditional value at risk.

For this kind of UQ problem, the most common non-intrusive methods are the method of moments, polynomial chaos, kriging, and Monte Carlo. The method of moments computes the statistical moments of the QoI analytically with a Taylor series approximation. It often only uses function evaluations and derivative information at one input point or a small number of them. The variants used most often use derivatives up to first or second order so that they stay cost-effective. This approach is efficient at estimating statistical moments, but it has difficulties estimating other kinds of risk measures, and it can be inaccurate when the input variance is large. The Monte Carlo approach instead samples the uncertain inputs randomly to compute the risk measures. Because of the law of large numbers, the convergence rate of Monte Carlo does not depend on the number of uncertain inputs, so it is particularly attractive for high-dimensional problems. Recent work to make it more efficient includes multi-fidelity and importance sampling techniques. But for low-dimensional problems, Monte Carlo can need many more model evaluations to get the same accuracy as the other UQ methods. Kriging, which is also known as Gaussian process regression, is a common statistical technique used in many fields. In UQ, kriging builds a surrogate response surface from input-output data pairs. The surrogate model replaces the original expensive function so that a large number of model evaluations can be done for reliability analysis or optimization under uncertainty. For low-dimensional UQ problems, if we assume the objective function is smooth, polynomial chaos-based techniques are often the most efficacious option. Generalized polynomial chaos theory represents the QoI with orthogonal polynomials derived from the distributions of the uncertain inputs. Since the random space is smooth, polynomial chaos-based methods converge fast with sampling or integration techniques. Common polynomial chaos-based methods are non-intrusive polynomial chaos (NIPC) and stochastic collocation (SC).

For both NIPC and SC we can sample the input space with a tensor-product grid, but this is often not preferred and is only used for very low-dimensional UQ problems, since the number of input points grows exponentially with the number of uncertain inputs. The commonly used methods sample the input space with a sparse grid or generate the sample points randomly, to reduce the number of input points while losing as little accuracy as possible. Our recent findings however show that keeping a tensor structure for the input points has some unique advantages, and for certain problems the total cost of model evaluations can be reduced in a different way without changing the tensor structure of the input points.

When a computational model is evaluated on full-grid input points, and we view the model as a computational graph with only elementary operations, the current framework evaluates every operation the same number of times, at the tensor-product input points of all the uncertain inputs. But for each operation, the output data only has distinct values at the distinct input points of its dependent input space, and many of the operations may not depend on all of the uncertain inputs. So the current framework of NIPC and SC can create a lot of wasteful evaluations for many of the operations.

In this paper we propose a computational graph transformation method called Accelerated Model evaluations on Tensor grids using Computational graph transformations (AMTC). It modifies the computational graph algorithmically to remove the unnecessary evaluations caused by the current framework of integration-based NIPC and SC. AMTC reduces the cost of model evaluation on full-grid quadrature points by partitioning the computational graph into sub-graphs using the dependency information of the operations, and then evaluating each sub-graph on the distinct quadrature points. The method is implemented together with a new algebraic modeling language, the Computational System Design Language (CSDL). We get the cost reductions on UQ problems in a general and automatic way by analyzing and manipulating the computational graph that CSDL makes available.

We applied this method to four different UQ problems with different computational graph structures. For three of the problems, model evaluation time was significantly accelerated when solving the UQ problems with the full-grid NIPC method, which makes this UQ method the most efficient of the implemented UQ methods for these problems. In general, we expect our method to significantly reduce model evaluation time on tensor-grid input points for a wide range of UQ problems involving multi-point, multi-disciplinary or other models with a sparse graph structure, and this can improve the time scaling for NIPC and SC methods but is not limited to them.

The paper is organized as follows. Section 2 gives background on PCE-related UQ methods, the current model evaluation framework, and how tensor-grid evaluations can be viewed through computational graphs. Section 3 presents the details of the new computational graph transformation algorithm, AMTC, and how it is implemented in CSDL. Section 4 shows the numerical results for three UQ problems. Section 5 summarizes the work and gives concluding thoughts.

steps.text:
In practical scenarios, numerical models inherently fall short of perfect fidelity with reality and must contend with inherent uncertainties. To address this challenge, uncertainty propagation, also known as forward uncertainty quantification (UQ), aims to rigorously examine and analyze how a system's output is influenced by the uncertainties in its inputs. The resulting uncertainty assessments serve as a valuable foundation for informed decision-making and thorough risk assessment. Applications of UQ can be found in many scientific and engineering domains, such as weather forecast [1,2], structural analysis [3,4] and aircraft design [5,6,7].

Input uncertainties can stem from diverse origins and are typically classified into two categories: aleatoric and epistemic. Aleatoric uncertainties, recognized as irreducible, are intrinsic to the system and encompass factors such as fluctuations in operational conditions, mission prerequisites, and model parameters; they can often be described within a probabilistic framework. In contrast, epistemic uncertainties are reducible uncertainties arising from knowledge gaps. They may be induced by approximations in computational models or numerical solution methods, and are often difficult to describe within a probabilistic framework. This paper focuses on UQ problems within a probabilistic formalism, where uncertain inputs are continuous random variables with known probability density distributions. The goal is to estimate statistical moments such as the mean and variance of the Quantity of Interest (QoI), or more complex risk measures such as the probability of failure or the conditional value at risk.

While efficient at estimating statistical moments, this approach struggles to estimate other kinds of risk measures, and it may lack accuracy when the input variance is significant. In contrast, the Monte Carlo approach uses random sampling of the uncertain inputs to compute the risk measures. By the law of large numbers, Monte Carlo's convergence rate is independent of the number of uncertain inputs, making it particularly attractive for high-dimensional problems. Recent efforts to improve its efficiency include multi-fidelity [12,13] and importance sampling [14] techniques. However, for low-dimensional problems, the Monte Carlo method may require substantially more model evaluations to reach the same accuracy as alternative UQ methods. Kriging, also known as Gaussian process regression, is a common statistical technique used in many fields. In UQ, kriging constructs a surrogate response surface from input-output data pairs; the surrogate replaces the original expensive function, allowing a large number of model evaluations for reliability analysis [15,16] or optimization under uncertainty [17]. For low-dimensional UQ problems, if the objective function is assumed to be smooth, polynomial chaos-based techniques often stand out as the most efficacious option. Generalized polynomial chaos theory represents the QoI with orthogonal polynomials derived from the distributions of the uncertain inputs. Benefiting from the smoothness of the random space, polynomial chaos-based methods exhibit rapid convergence with sampling or integration techniques. Common polynomial chaos-based methods include non-intrusive polynomial chaos (NIPC) [18,19,20] and stochastic collocation (SC) [21,22].

For both NIPC and SC, a tensor-product grid can be used to sample the input space, but this approach is often not preferred and is used only for very low-dimensional UQ problems, as the number of input points increases exponentially with the number of uncertain inputs. Commonly used methods instead sample the input space with a sparse grid or generate the sample points randomly, reducing the number of input points with minimal loss of accuracy. However, our recent findings show that maintaining a tensor structure for the input points offers some unique advantages, and for certain problems the total model evaluation cost can be reduced through a different approach without changing that tensor structure.

When a computational model is evaluated on full-grid input points and viewed as a computational graph of elementary operations, the current framework evaluates each operation the same number of times, at the tensor-product input points of all the uncertain inputs. However, the output of each operation only has distinct values at the distinct input points of its dependent input space, and a large portion of the operations may not depend on all of the uncertain inputs. This means the current NIPC and SC framework can incur many wasteful evaluations across a large portion of the operations.

In this paper, we propose a computational graph transformation method called Accelerated Model evaluations on Tensor grids using Computational graph transformations (AMTC), which algorithmically modifies the computational graph to eliminate the unnecessary evaluations incurred by the current framework of integration-based NIPC and SC. AMTC reduces the model evaluation cost on full-grid quadrature points by partitioning the computational graph into sub-graphs according to the operations' dependency information and evaluating each sub-graph on its distinct quadrature points. The method is implemented in conjunction with a new algebraic modeling language, the Computational System Design Language (CSDL), and achieves cost reductions on UQ problems in a general and automatic way by analyzing and manipulating the computational graph that CSDL makes available.

We applied this method to four different UQ problems with different computational graph structures. For three of the problems, we observed a significant acceleration in model evaluation time when solving the UQ problems with the full-grid NIPC method, making it the most efficient of the implemented UQ methods for these problems. More generally, for a wide range of UQ problems involving multi-point, multi-disciplinary, or other models with a sparse graph structure, we expect our method to significantly reduce model evaluation time on tensor-grid input points, improving the time scaling of NIPC and SC methods, among others.

This paper is organized as follows. Section 2 provides background on PCE-related UQ methods, the current model evaluation framework, and how tensor-grid evaluations can be viewed through computational graphs. Section 3 presents the details of the new computational graph transformation algorithm, AMTC, and its implementation in CSDL. Section 4 shows the numerical results of three UQ problems. Section 5 summarizes the work and offers concluding thoughts.
